Lake Malawi, also called Lake Nyasa, is an East African lake spanning approximately eleven thousand four hundred square miles along the borders of Tanzania, Mozambique, and Malawi. The third-largest lake in Africa by surface area, it is renowned for its extraordinary diversity of endemic fish species and plays a vital role in the region's food security.

The lake stretches roughly three hundred sixty miles from north to south, with an average width of forty miles, making it one of Africa's most elongated lakes. It contains more fish species—over a thousand—than any other lake in the world, most found nowhere else, and these species support major artisanal fisheries. Located in the East African Rift Valley, it shares the same tectonic origin as Lakes Tanganyika and Victoria.

Known locally as Lake Nyasa in Tanzania and Mozambique, the nation of Malawi has adopted "Lake Malawi" as the standard English name. The lake's waters are among the clearest of Africa's great lakes, allowing sunlight to penetrate to remarkable depths. Over four million people depend on its fisheries for protein and income, though overfishing is a growing concern. The shoreline includes significant conservation areas and is increasingly a focus of ecotourism.
